notes.front: What is a reciprocating engine?
notes.back: An engine whose pistons move back and forth in cylinders, turning the chemical energy of fuel into mechanical energy.
notes.explanation: The name comes from that back-and-forth, or reciprocating, movement of the pistons; most small aircraft are designed with this type of engine.
notes.example: Like the petrol engine in a car, but turning a propeller instead of the wheels.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Reciprocating Engines”, p. 7-2
notes.evidence: Most small aircraft are designed with reciprocating engines. The name is derived from the back-and-forth, or reciprocating, movement of the pistons that produces the mechanical energy necessary to accomplish work.

notes.front: What is the four-stroke cycle?
notes.back: The operating cycle in which intake, compression, power and exhaust each take a separate stroke of the piston, in that order.
notes.explanation: Spark-ignition four-stroke engines remain the most common design used in general aviation today.
notes.example: Like a rower’s stroke broken into four fixed moves (catch, drive, finish, recovery), each doing one job before the cycle repeats.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Reciprocating Engines”, p. 7-3
notes.evidence: The intake, compression, power, and exhaust processes occur in four separate strokes of the piston in the following order.

notes.front: What is a fixed-pitch propeller?
notes.back: A propeller whose blade angle is set by the manufacturer and cannot be changed.
notes.explanation: It achieves its best efficiency only at one combination of airspeed and rpm, so its pitch is ideal for neither cruise nor climb.
notes.example: Like a bicycle with a single gear: simple and light, but never quite right for both hills and flat roads.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Fixed-Pitch Propeller”, p. 7-5
notes.evidence: The pitch of this propeller is set by the manufacturer and

notes.front: What is a constant-speed propeller?
notes.back: A controllable-pitch propeller whose pitch a governor varies automatically in flight to hold the selected rpm despite varying air loads.
notes.explanation: It is the most common type of adjustable-pitch propeller, and it lets the pilot select the most efficient engine rpm for the conditions.
notes.example: Like cruise control that holds a car’s engine speed by changing gear for you as the road rises and falls.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Adjustable-Pitch Propeller”, p. 7-6
notes.evidence: whose pitch is automatically varied in flight by a governor

notes.front: What is manifold pressure (MP)?
notes.back: The absolute pressure of the fuel-air mixture in the engine’s intake manifold, shown on the manifold pressure gauge.
notes.explanation: With a constant-speed propeller, power output is controlled by the throttle and indicated by this gauge; more throttle lets more fuel and air in and the reading rises.
notes.example: Like a pressure gauge fitted to the engine’s intake pipe: open the throttle and the reading climbs towards the outside air pressure.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Adjustable-Pitch Propeller”, p. 7-6
notes.evidence: The gauge measures the absolute pressure of the fuel-air mixture inside the intake manifold and is more

notes.front: What is a float-type carburetor?
notes.back: A carburettor in which a float resting on fuel in the float chamber opens and closes a needle valve that meters fuel to the engine.
notes.explanation: Air flowing through the venturi creates low pressure that draws fuel into the airstream; the float type is the more common of the two carburettor types.
notes.example: Like the float valve in a toilet cistern that shuts off the water as the level rises, but metering fuel for an engine.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Carburetor Systems”, p. 7-8
notes.evidence: float that rests on fuel within the float chamber.

notes.front: What is fuel injection?
notes.back: An induction system that injects fuel directly into the cylinders, or just ahead of the intake valves, instead of mixing it in a carburettor.
notes.explanation: A fuel-air control unit essentially replaces the carburettor: it meters fuel by the mixture setting and sends it on at a rate set by the throttle.
notes.example: Like a spray nozzle at each cylinder’s doorway, instead of one mixing bowl feeding the whole engine.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Fuel Injection Systems”, p. 7-11
notes.evidence: the cylinders, or just ahead of the intake valve.

notes.front: What is the mixture control?
notes.back: The flight-deck control that adjusts the fuel-air ratio; the carburettor is calibrated for sea level with the mixture set full rich.
notes.explanation: Because the setting that is right at sea level is wrong higher up, the pilot must lean or enrich the mixture as the air density changes.
notes.example: Like the gas knob on a camping stove, turned to match the fuel to the air the burner is actually getting.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Mixture Control”, p. 7-9
notes.evidence: mixture control set in the FULL RICH position.

notes.front: What is carburetor icing?
notes.back: Ice forming inside the carburettor, mainly around the throttle valve and venturi throat, from the sharp temperature drop there.
notes.explanation: Fuel vaporisation and the drop in air pressure in the venturi cool the air sharply; if water vapour condenses at or below freezing, ice forms, restricting the mixture flow and reducing power.
notes.example: Like the frost that forms on an aerosol can’s nozzle after a long spray, even on a warm day.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Carburetor Icing”, p. 7-9
notes.evidence: pressure in the venturi, which causes a sharp temperature

notes.front: What is carburetor heat?
notes.back: An anti-icing system that preheats the air before it reaches the carburettor, to keep the fuel-air mixture above freezing.
notes.explanation: It can melt ice that has already formed if there is not too much, but the handbook says using it as a preventative measure is the better option.
notes.example: Like running a hair-dryer over a pipe before a frost rather than after it has frozen solid.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Carburetor Heat”, p. 7-10
notes.evidence: Carburetor heat is an anti-icing system that preheats the air before it reaches the carburetor and is intended to keep the

notes.front: What is a magneto?
notes.back: A device that uses a permanent magnet to generate the ignition current, completely independently of the aircraft’s electrical system.
notes.explanation: It makes a high enough voltage to jump a spark across each spark plug gap, and it keeps working whenever the crankshaft is turning.
notes.example: Like a bicycle dynamo that lights the lamp from the turning wheel, with no battery involved.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Ignition System”, p. 7-15
notes.evidence: A magneto uses a permanent magnet to generate an electrical

notes.front: What is detonation?
notes.back: An uncontrolled, explosive ignition of the fuel-air mixture within the cylinder’s combustion chamber.
notes.explanation: It causes excessive temperatures and pressures that, if not corrected, can quickly lead to failure of the piston, cylinder or valves.
notes.example: Like a firework going off all at once instead of a candle burning steadily down from its wick.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Combustion”, p. 7-19
notes.evidence: fuel-air mixture within the cylinder’s combustion chamber.

notes.front: What is preignition?
notes.back: Ignition of the fuel-air mixture before the engine’s normal ignition event, usually from a residual hot spot in the combustion chamber.
notes.explanation: The hot spot is often a small carbon deposit on a spark plug, a cracked spark plug insulator or other damage that heats a part enough to ignite the charge.
notes.example: Like a starting pistol that fires before the starter has pulled the trigger.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Combustion”, p. 7-19
notes.evidence: Preignition occurs when the fuel-air mixture ignites prior

notes.front: What is vapor lock?
notes.back: Air or fuel vapour in the fuel system that stops fuel reaching the cylinders and makes the engine difficult to restart.
notes.explanation: Running a tank completely dry can let air into the fuel system; on fuel-injected engines the fuel can get so hot that it vaporises in the fuel line.
notes.example: Like an air bubble in a drinking straw: you suck, but no drink comes up.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Fuel Selectors”, p. 7-26
notes.evidence: to enter the fuel system and cause vapor lock, which makes

notes.front: What is a turbocharger?
notes.back: A compressor driven by a turbine in the engine’s exhaust stream, which pressurises the intake air so the engine can keep its power at altitude.
notes.explanation: A supercharger does the same job but is driven by the engine itself; the turbocharger instead uses exhaust energy that would otherwise be lost.
notes.example: Like a windmill in the exhaust pipe that drives a fan blowing extra air into the intake.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Superchargers and Turbosuperchargers”, p. 7-12
notes.evidence: air pump or compressor, while a turbocharger gets its power

notes.front: What is the alternator?
notes.back: The engine-driven source of electric current for the aircraft’s electrical system, which also keeps the battery charged.
notes.explanation: The battery then provides power for starting and a limited supply of power if the alternator fails.
notes.example: Like a phone charger that keeps the battery topped up while you use the phone, but turned by the engine.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Electrical System”, p. 7-30
notes.evidence: Engine-driven alternators or generators supply electric

notes.front: What is the ammeter?
notes.back: An instrument that shows whether the alternator is producing enough electrical power and whether the battery is being charged.
notes.explanation: Its zero is in the centre of the face, with a positive indication on one side and a negative one on the other.
notes.example: Like the charging arrow on a phone’s battery icon, but showing how fast current flows into or out of the battery.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Electrical System”, p. 7-31
notes.evidence: The ammeter shows if the alternator/ generator is producing an adequate supply of electrical power.

notes.front: What does the master switch do?
notes.back: It turns the electrical system on or off; switched on, it powers all electrical equipment circuits except the ignition system.
notes.explanation: The ignition does not depend on it: the magnetos need no outside source of electrical power.
notes.example: Like the main switch in a house’s fuse box: it cuts the lights and sockets, but not a wind-up clock.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Electrical System”, p. 7-30
notes.evidence: electrical energy to all the electrical equipment circuits

notes.front: What is a circuit breaker?
notes.back: A device that protects circuits and equipment from electrical overload, like a fuse, but that can be reset by hand instead of replaced.
notes.explanation: Placards at the breaker or fuse panel name each circuit and show its amperage limit.
notes.example: Like the trip switch in a home’s consumer unit that you flick back up after an overloaded kettle trips it.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Electrical System”, p. 7-31
notes.evidence: have the same function as a fuse but can be manually reset

notes.front: What is cylinder head temperature (CHT)?
notes.back: The temperature of the engine’s cylinders, shown by a gauge that gives a direct and immediate indication of any change.
notes.explanation: The gauge is usually colour coded with a green arc for the normal range and a red line for the maximum allowable temperature.
notes.example: Like a thermometer stuck on the side of a pan rather than one in the cooling water: it reacts at once when the pan heats.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Engine Cooling Systems”, p. 7-18
notes.evidence: gauge that indicates a direct and immediate cylinder

notes.front: What is the engine oil system?
notes.back: The system that lubricates the engine, cools it, seals between cylinder walls and pistons, and carries away contaminants.
notes.explanation: Reciprocating engines use either a wet-sump system, with the oil in a sump that is part of the engine, or a dry-sump system with a separate oil tank.
notes.example: Like the oil in a car engine: as it circulates it lubricates, cools, seals and cleans.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Oil Systems”, p. 7-16
notes.evidence: oil system. In a wet-sump system, the oil is located in a sump that

notes.front: What is an aviation fuel grade?
notes.back: The octane or performance number of aviation gasoline, which designates its antiknock value: its resistance to knocking in the cylinder.
notes.explanation: The higher the grade, the more pressure the fuel can withstand without detonating, so higher grades are used in higher-compression engines.
notes.example: Like the octane numbers on petrol pumps, but for aviation gasoline, with each grade dyed its own colour.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Fuel Grades”, p. 7-27
notes.evidence: performance number (grade), which designates the antiknock value or knock resistance of the fuel mixture in the engine

notes.front: What is pitot heat?
notes.back: Electrical heating of the pitot tube to keep it free of ice; it is the only ice protection most light aircraft have.
notes.explanation: Most light aircraft with only a heated pitot tube are not certified for flight in icing conditions.
notes.example: Like a heated car wing-mirror that stops frost forming, but keeping the airspeed sensor’s opening clear.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Anti-Ice and Deice Systems”, p. 7-40
notes.evidence: Most light aircraft have only a heated pitot tube and are not certified for flight in icing.

notes.front: What is a supplemental oxygen system?
notes.back: A fixed or portable system that supplies oxygen through a mask or cannula, with a regulator that sets the flow by cabin altitude.
notes.explanation: Crew and passengers use oxygen systems, with pressurisation where it is fitted, to prevent oxygen deficiency (hypoxia) at altitude.
notes.example: Like a diver’s regulator, but topping up the cabin air with oxygen rather than replacing it.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Oxygen Systems”, p. 7-37
notes.evidence: An oxygen system consists of a mask or cannula and a

notes.front: What is cabin pressurization?
notes.back: A sealed cabin kept at a higher pressure than outside, typically holding a cabin altitude of about 8,000 feet at the maximum designed cruising altitude.
notes.explanation: Air leaves through an outflow valve, which regulates the exit so that a constant inflow of air to the pressurised area is possible.
notes.example: Like a sealed bottle that keeps its fizz on a mountain top: the inside stays at a lower-altitude pressure than the air around it.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Pressurized Aircraft”, p. 7-35
notes.evidence: pressure altitude of approximately 8,000 feet at the maximum

notes.front: What is the landing gear?
notes.back: The principal support of the aircraft on the surface: most commonly wheels, though floats or skis can be fitted.
notes.explanation: On small aircraft it is two main wheels plus a third wheel at either the nose (tricycle gear) or the tail (conventional gear).
notes.example: Like the legs and castors of an office chair, one of which can be steered.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Landing Gear”, p. 7-33
notes.evidence: of wheels, but aircraft can also be equipped with floats for

notes.front: What is the difference between anti-ice and deice equipment?
notes.back: Anti-icing equipment prevents ice from forming; deicing equipment removes ice after it has formed.
notes.explanation: These systems protect places such as wing and tail leading edges, pitot and static openings, fuel vents, windshields and propeller blades.
notes.example: Like gritting a road before a frost (anti-ice) versus scraping a frozen windscreen in the morning (deice).
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Anti-Ice and Deice Systems”, p. 7-40
notes.evidence: of ice, while deicing equipment is designed to remove ice once it has formed.

notes.front: The piston is travelling downwards with the intake valve open, drawing fuel-air mixture into the cylinder. Which stroke of the four-stroke cycle is this?
notes.back: The intake stroke.
notes.explanation: The intake stroke begins as the piston starts downwards and the intake valve opens; the compression stroke starts when that valve closes and the piston rises.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Reciprocating Engines”, p. 7-3
notes.evidence: The intake stroke begins as the piston starts its downward travel. When this happens, the intake valve opens and the fuel-air mixture is drawn into the cylinder.

notes.front: Why is a propeller blade twisted, with the greatest angle at the hub and the smallest at the tip?
notes.back: To produce uniform lift from hub to tip, because the tip travels faster than the part near the hub.
notes.explanation: A blade with one angle all along would be inefficient: at speed the part near the hub would have a negative angle of attack while the tip was stalled.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Propeller”, p. 7-4
notes.evidence: The reason for the twist is to produce uniform lift from the hub to the tip.

notes.front: In an aircraft with a fixed-pitch propeller, which instrument indicates engine power?
notes.back: The tachometer, which gives a direct reading of engine and propeller rpm.
notes.explanation: The rpm is regulated by the throttle, and at a given altitude a higher tachometer reading means more power.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Fixed-Pitch Propeller”, p. 7-5
notes.evidence: In a fixed-pitch propeller, the tachometer is the indicator of

notes.front: Why does 2,300 rpm at 5,000 feet produce less horsepower than 2,300 rpm at sea level?
notes.back: Power output depends on air density, and air density decreases as altitude increases.
notes.explanation: So as altitude increases, the throttle must be opened further to show the same rpm as at a lower altitude.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Fixed-Pitch Propeller”, p. 7-5
notes.evidence: at sea level because power output depends on air density.

notes.front: In an aircraft with a constant-speed propeller, what do the throttle and the propeller control each do?
notes.back: The throttle controls power output (shown as manifold pressure); the propeller control regulates engine rpm.
notes.explanation: The rpm set with the propeller control is shown on the tachometer.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Adjustable-Pitch Propeller”, p. 7-6
notes.evidence: power output, and the propeller control regulates engine

notes.front: How does an engine failure or power loss show on the manifold pressure gauge?
notes.back: As an increase in manifold pressure to the ambient air pressure at the altitude where the failure happened.
notes.explanation: While the engine runs, manifold pressure sits below the ambient pressure; with the engine stopped, the gauge reads ambient pressure.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Adjustable-Pitch Propeller”, p. 7-6
notes.evidence: pressure to a value corresponding to the ambient air pressure

notes.front: With a constant-speed propeller, which do you reduce first when decreasing power: MP or rpm?
notes.back: Reduce manifold pressure first, then rpm.
notes.explanation: If rpm is reduced first, manifold pressure automatically increases and may exceed the manufacturer’s tolerances.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Adjustable-Pitch Propeller”, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: manifold pressure before reducing rpm.

notes.front: Cruising with a constant-speed propeller, you want to go from 24 inches and 2,400 rpm to 20 inches and 2,200 rpm. What order do you use?
notes.back: A) Throttle back to 20 inches first, then propeller control back to 2,200 rpm.
notes.choices:
A) Throttle back to 20 inches first, then propeller control back to 2,200 rpm
B) Propeller control back to 2,200 rpm first, then throttle back to 20 inches
C) Move both together; the order does not matter
notes.choicesExplained: B: reducing rpm first makes manifold pressure rise, possibly past the manufacturer’s tolerances. C: the handbook gives a set order for changing both.
notes.explanation: When power settings are being decreased, manifold pressure is reduced before rpm.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Adjustable-Pitch Propeller”, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: manifold pressure before reducing rpm.

notes.front: In a fixed-pitch aircraft you cruise at 2,300 rpm near sea level, then climb to 6,000 feet and again set 2,300 rpm. Compared with before, what is true?
notes.back: A) The throttle is further open, and the engine produces less horsepower.
notes.choices:
A) The throttle is further open, and the engine produces less horsepower
B) The throttle position and horsepower are the same, because rpm is the same
C) The throttle is closed further, because thinner air needs less
notes.choicesExplained: B: the same rpm at altitude gives less power, because power depends on air density. C: the throttle must be opened further, not closed, to hold rpm as altitude increases.
notes.explanation: Power output depends on air density, and to show the same rpm higher up the throttle must be opened further.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Fixed-Pitch Propeller”, p. 7-6
notes.evidence: increased, the throttle must be opened further to indicate the

notes.front: What is the chief disadvantage of the float-type carburettor?
notes.back: Its tendency to ice.
notes.explanation: It also does not work well in abrupt manoeuvres, and its low-pressure fuel discharge vaporises incompletely.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Carburetor Systems”, p. 7-8
notes.evidence: disadvantage of the float-type carburetor, however, is its

notes.front: Where does carburettor ice generally form?
notes.back: Near the throttle valve and in the venturi throat.
notes.explanation: Ice there restricts the flow of the fuel-air mixture and reduces power; if enough builds up, the engine may stop.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Carburetor Icing”, p. 7-9
notes.evidence: generally forms in the vicinity of the throttle valve and in the

notes.front: Carburettor ice is most likely below what temperature and above what relative humidity?
notes.back: Below 21 °C (70 °F) with relative humidity above 80 percent.
notes.explanation: These are the most likely conditions, not the only ones: the chart in the handbook notes icing is possible outside them.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Carburetor Icing”, p. 7-9
notes.evidence: degrees Celsius (°C) and the relative humidity is above 80 percent.

notes.front: What is the first indication of carburettor ice in an aircraft with a fixed-pitch propeller?
notes.back: A decrease in engine rpm, which may be followed by engine roughness.
notes.explanation: With a fixed-pitch propeller the tachometer is the power indicator, so lost power shows there first.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Carburetor Icing”, p. 7-10
notes.evidence: a fixed-pitch propeller is a decrease in engine rpm, which

notes.front: How is carburettor ice usually indicated in an aircraft with a constant-speed propeller?
notes.back: A decrease in manifold pressure, but no reduction in rpm.
notes.explanation: Propeller pitch is adjusted automatically to make up for the loss of power, so rpm stays constant.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Carburetor Icing”, p. 7-10
notes.evidence: by a decrease in manifold pressure, but no reduction in rpm.

notes.front: When is carburettor ice particularly dangerous?
notes.back: When using reduced power during a descent, because it can build unnoticed until power is added.
notes.explanation: Carburettor ice can occur in any phase of flight, but low power hides its effect.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Carburetor Icing”, p. 7-10
notes.evidence: particularly dangerous when using reduced power during a

notes.front: Why does carburettor heat reduce engine power, and by how much?
notes.back: The heated air is less dense than outside air, which enriches the mixture; power can fall by up to 15 percent.
notes.explanation: For the same reason it also raises the engine’s operating temperature.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Carburetor Heat”, p. 7-10
notes.evidence: air is less dense than the outside air that had been entering

notes.front: With a fixed-pitch propeller, how does rpm respond to carburettor heat if ice is present?
notes.back: Rpm decreases, then gradually increases as the ice melts; the engine should then run more smoothly.
notes.explanation: The first drop comes from the less dense heated air; the recovery comes as melting ice stops restricting the flow.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Carburetor Heat”, p. 7-10
notes.evidence: a gradual increase in rpm as the ice melts.

notes.front: After you apply full carburettor heat to clear ice, the engine runs rougher for a while. What should you do?
notes.back: Keep carburettor heat in the full-hot position until normal power returns.
notes.explanation: Full heat further reduces power and may cause roughness as melted ice goes through the engine; this may last from 30 seconds to several minutes.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Carburetor Heat”, p. 7-10
notes.evidence: This is accomplished by applying full carburetor heat, which will further reduce power and may cause engine

notes.front: If carburettor icing is suspected and a closed-throttle descent is planned, when should carburettor heat go on?
notes.back: Full on before closing the throttle, and left on during the closed-throttle operation.
notes.explanation: With the throttle closed the engine cools rapidly and fuel vaporises less completely, so it is more susceptible to icing.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Carburetor Heat”, p. 7-10
notes.evidence: throttle and leave it on during the closed-throttle operation.

notes.front: Why should carburettor heat not be used during takeoff?
notes.back: It reduces engine output and increases operating temperature, and takeoff needs full power.
notes.explanation: In normal operation it is used only to check for, or to remove, carburettor ice.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Carburetor Heat”, p. 7-11
notes.evidence: of the engine and to increase the operating temperature

notes.front: On a cool, damp morning your fixed-pitch aircraft slowly loses rpm in level cruise with the throttle unchanged. What is the likely cause and first action?
notes.back: A) Carburettor ice: apply full carburettor heat and leave it on.
notes.choices:
A) Carburettor ice: apply full carburettor heat and leave it on
B) A failing magneto: switch to one magneto
C) Rich mixture at altitude: apply partial carburettor heat
notes.choicesExplained: B: one failed magneto causes only a slight power drop, and switching magnetos in cruise is not the remedy. C: partial heat may aggravate ice, and a gradual rpm loss in these conditions points to ice.
notes.explanation: A decrease in rpm is the first sign of carburettor ice with a fixed-pitch propeller, and detected ice calls for full heat at once.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Carburetor Icing”, p. 7-10
notes.evidence: a fixed-pitch propeller is a decrease in engine rpm, which

notes.front: Is a fuel-injected engine free of induction icing?
notes.back: No. It is less susceptible than a carburettor system, but impact icing on the air intake is possible in either system.
notes.explanation: Impact icing is ice that forms on the outside of the aircraft and blocks openings such as the air intake.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Fuel Injection Systems”, p. 7-12
notes.evidence: A fuel injection system is considered to be less susceptible to icing than a carburetor system, but impact icing on the air

notes.front: What are two advantages of fuel injection over a carburettor?
notes.back: Any two, for example reduced evaporative icing and faster throttle response.
notes.explanation: The handbook also lists better fuel flow, precise control of mixture, better fuel distribution and easier cold-weather starts.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Fuel Injection Systems”, p. 7-12
notes.evidence: • Faster throttle response

notes.front: On a hot afternoon you stop for fuel and, ten minutes later, your fuel-injected engine is reluctant to start. Which listed disadvantage of fuel injection is this?
notes.back: C) Difficulty in starting a hot engine.
notes.choices:
A) Impact icing on the air intake
B) Imprecise mixture control
C) Difficulty in starting a hot engine
notes.choicesExplained: A: impact icing is ice on the outside of the aircraft, not a hot-day problem. B: precise mixture control is listed as an advantage of fuel injection.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists difficulty in starting a hot engine, and vapour locks on hot days, among the disadvantages of fuel injection.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Fuel Injection Systems”, p. 7-12
notes.evidence: • Difficulty in starting a hot engine

notes.front: Why does the mixture get richer as altitude increases if it is not adjusted?
notes.back: The density of the air entering the carburettor decreases while the density of the fuel stays the same.
notes.explanation: Leaning decreases fuel flow, which compensates for the lower air density at altitude.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Mixture Control”, p. 7-9
notes.evidence: altitude increases, the density of air entering the carburetor decreases, while the density of the fuel remains the same.

notes.front: What does a progressively over-rich mixture at altitude cause?
notes.back: Engine roughness and an appreciable loss of power, normally from spark plugs fouled by carbon.
notes.explanation: The rich mixture lowers the temperature inside the cylinder, inhibiting complete combustion, so carbon builds up on the plugs.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Mixture Control”, p. 7-9
notes.evidence: roughness and an appreciable loss of power. The roughness normally is due to spark plug fouling from excessive carbon buildup on the plugs.

notes.front: What must you do with the mixture during a descent from high altitude, and why?
notes.back: Enrich it; otherwise it may become too lean, and an overly lean mixture causes detonation.
notes.explanation: The handbook says the best way to keep the proper mixture is to monitor engine temperature and enrich as needed.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Mixture Control”, p. 7-9
notes.evidence: During a descent from high altitude, the fuel-air mixture must be enriched, or it may become too lean. An overly lean mixture causes detonation

notes.front: Doing your run-up at a mountain airport at 7,000 feet, the engine runs rough with the mixture full rich. What does the handbook point to?
notes.back: C) A mixture too rich for the thin air; lean it as the flight manual directs.
notes.choices:
A) Carburettor ice; apply partial heat and take off
B) A lean mixture; leave it full rich
C) A mixture too rich for the thin air; lean it as the flight manual directs
notes.choicesExplained: A: partial heat can aggravate ice, and the run-up at a high airport is the handbook’s example of an over-rich mixture. B: full rich is already the richest setting, so the mixture cannot be too lean.
notes.explanation: At high-elevation airports the sea-level mixture setting is too rich, which fouls the plugs and makes the engine rough.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Mixture Control”, p. 7-9
notes.evidence: airports and during climbs or cruise flight at high altitudes.

notes.front: What is a turbocharged engine’s critical altitude?
notes.back: The maximum altitude at which it can produce its rated horsepower.
notes.explanation: Above it, power output begins to decrease as it does for a normally aspirated engine.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Turbosuperchargers”, p. 7-13
notes.evidence: a turbocharged engine can produce its rated horsepower.

notes.front: If one magneto fails in flight, what happens to the engine?
notes.back: It keeps running normally, with a slight decrease in power.
notes.explanation: The other magneto is unaffected; the same is true if one of the two spark plugs in a cylinder fails.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Ignition System”, p. 7-15
notes.evidence: although a slight decrease in engine power can be expected.

notes.front: How is the ignition system checked before takeoff?
notes.back: Watch the rpm drop as the ignition switch is moved from both to right, and then from both to left.
notes.explanation: A small drop is normal; the permissible drop is listed in the POH.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Ignition System”, p. 7-15
notes.evidence: occurs when the ignition switch is first moved from BOTH to RIGHT and then from BOTH to LEFT.

notes.front: During the magneto check, which two results mean you must not fly until the problem is fixed?
notes.back: The engine stops when switched to one magneto, or the rpm drop exceeds the allowable limit.
notes.explanation: Possible causes include fouled plugs, broken or shorted wires between magneto and plugs, or improperly timed firing of the plugs.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Ignition System”, p. 7-15
notes.evidence: running when switched to one magneto or if the rpm drop

notes.front: Is “no drop” in rpm during the magneto check a good sign?
notes.back: No. It is not normal, and the aircraft should not be flown.
notes.explanation: A small decrease in rpm on each single magneto is what a normal system shows.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Ignition System”, p. 7-16
notes.evidence: that “no drop” in rpm is not normal, and in that instance, the

notes.front: After shutdown, the battery and master switches are off but the ignition switch was left on. What is the danger?
notes.back: The engine can fire and turn over if the propeller is moved, because the magneto needs no outside electrical power.
notes.explanation: The handbook warns of the potential for serious injury, so the ignition switch goes to off after shutdown.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Ignition System”, p. 7-16
notes.evidence: OFF, the engine can fire and turn over if the ignition switch

notes.front: Your POH allows a 150 rpm drop on each magneto. At the run-up you see 75 rpm on the right and 250 rpm on the left. What do you do?
notes.back: C) Do not fly until the problem is corrected.
notes.choices:
A) Take off: the average drop is within limits
B) Take off on both magnetos: the right one works
C) Do not fly until the problem is corrected
notes.choicesExplained: A: the limit applies to each magneto, and the left drop exceeds it. B: a drop beyond the allowable limit means the aircraft is not flown, whatever the other magneto shows.
notes.explanation: An rpm drop that exceeds the allowable limit on either magneto means the aircraft is not flown until fixed.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Ignition System”, p. 7-15
notes.evidence: exceeds the allowable limit, do not fly the aircraft until

notes.front: A high oil temperature may point to a problem with which component whose job is to cool the oil?
notes.back: A blocked oil cooler.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists it with a plugged oil line, a low oil quantity and a defective temperature gauge.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Oil Systems”, p. 7-17
notes.evidence: line, a low oil quantity, a blocked oil cooler, or a defective

notes.front: Which oil quantity problem can show up as a high oil temperature?
notes.back: A low oil quantity.
notes.explanation: The oil level is checked on the dipstick during the preflight inspection and topped up to the manufacturer’s levels.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Oil Systems”, p. 7-17
notes.evidence: line, a low oil quantity, a blocked oil cooler, or a defective

notes.front: Which blockage in the oil plumbing can cause a high oil temperature indication?
notes.back: A plugged oil line.
notes.explanation: It is one of four possible causes the handbook lists for a high oil temperature indication.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Oil Systems”, p. 7-17
notes.evidence: High oil temperature indications may signal a plugged oil

notes.front: Which instrument fault can give a high oil temperature reading with no real problem in the engine?
notes.back: A defective temperature gauge.
notes.explanation: It is one of four possible causes the handbook lists, beside a plugged oil line, a low oil quantity and a blocked oil cooler.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Oil Systems”, p. 7-17
notes.evidence: line, a low oil quantity, a blocked oil cooler, or a defective

notes.front: In cruise, your oil temperature creeps towards the red line. Which of these is a possible cause the handbook lists?
notes.back: A) A low oil quantity.
notes.choices:
A) A low oil quantity
B) Improper oil viscosity in cold weather
C) A fouled spark plug
notes.choicesExplained: B: improper viscosity in cold weather is listed as a cause of low, not high, oil temperature. C: a fouled plug shows as roughness or an rpm drop, not an oil temperature rise.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists low oil quantity among the possible causes of high oil temperature, with a plugged oil line, a blocked cooler and a faulty gauge.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Oil Systems”, p. 7-17
notes.evidence: line, a low oil quantity, a blocked oil cooler, or a defective

notes.front: When is an air-cooled engine’s cooling least effective?
notes.back: During ground operations, takeoffs, go-arounds and other periods of high power at low airspeed.
notes.explanation: Air cooling relies on outside air flowing into the cowling and over the fins on the cylinders.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Engine Cooling Systems”, p. 7-17
notes.evidence: The air cooling system is less effective during ground operations, takeoffs, go-arounds, and other periods of high-

notes.front: What three actions help reduce excessive cylinder head temperature?
notes.back: Increase airspeed, enrich the fuel-air mixture and/or reduce power.
notes.explanation: Any of these helps lower engine temperature; with cowl flaps, opening them also helps.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Engine Cooling Systems”, p. 7-18
notes.evidence: airspeed, enrich the fuel-air mixture, and/or reduce

notes.front: How are cowl flaps used to control engine temperature?
notes.back: Open them to lower a high engine temperature; close them to raise a low one.
notes.explanation: They are hinged covers over the opening where hot air leaves the cowling, so they set how much air flows through.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Engine Cooling Systems”, p. 7-18
notes.evidence: temperature is high, the cowl flaps can be opened to permit

notes.front: In a long, steep full-power climb on a hot day, CHT nears the red line. Which response fits the handbook?
notes.back: B) Lower the nose to gain airspeed, enrich the mixture and, if fitted, open the cowl flaps.
notes.choices:
A) Lean the mixture to cool the cylinders
B) Lower the nose to gain airspeed, enrich the mixture and, if fitted, open the cowl flaps
C) Close the cowl flaps to hold the heat in the engine
notes.choicesExplained: A: enriching, not leaning, is listed to reduce cylinder head temperature. C: closing cowl flaps restricts the flow of hot air and increases engine temperature.
notes.explanation: Increasing airspeed, enriching the mixture and reducing power all reduce cylinder head temperature, and open cowl flaps let more cooling air through.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Engine Cooling Systems”, p. 7-18
notes.evidence: airspeed, enrich the fuel-air mixture, and/or reduce

notes.front: What reading characterises detonation, and when is it most likely?
notes.back: High cylinder head temperatures; it is most likely at high power settings.
notes.explanation: In less severe cases detonation causes overheating, roughness or loss of power.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Combustion”, p. 7-19
notes.evidence: Detonation is characterized by high cylinder head temperatures

notes.front: Which fuel-related cause of detonation does the handbook list?
notes.back: Using a lower fuel grade than the aircraft manufacturer specifies.
notes.explanation: A lower grade withstands less pressure before detonating than the engine was designed for.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Combustion”, p. 7-19
notes.evidence: Use of a lower fuel grade than that specified by the

notes.front: Which combination of manifold pressure and rpm is a common cause of detonation?
notes.back: Extremely high manifold pressure with low rpm.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists it with a lower fuel grade, an excessively lean mixture at high power, and reduced cylinder cooling.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Combustion”, p. 7-19
notes.evidence: Operation of the engine with extremely high manifold

notes.front: Which mixture setting at high power is a common cause of detonation?
notes.back: An excessively lean mixture.
notes.explanation: The handbook gives the same warning for descents from altitude: without enriching, the mixture may become too lean and cause detonation.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Combustion”, p. 7-19
notes.evidence: Operation of the engine at high power settings with an excessively lean mixture

notes.front: Which operations that reduce cylinder cooling are a common cause of detonation?
notes.back: Extended ground operations or steep climbs.
notes.explanation: Cylinder cooling is reduced in both; avoiding extended, high-power, steep climbs is one of the handbook’s prevention guidelines.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Combustion”, p. 7-19
notes.evidence: Maintaining extended ground operations or steep

notes.front: What does preignition do to the engine?
notes.back: It causes a loss of power and high operating temperature, and may cause severe engine damage.
notes.explanation: The expanding gases push hard on the piston while it is still on its compression stroke.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Combustion”, p. 7-19
notes.evidence: Preignition causes the engine to lose power

notes.front: A pilot climbs steeply at full power on a hot day with the mixture leaned well back. CHT is high and the engine begins to run rough. What is most likely happening?
notes.back: A) Detonation.
notes.choices:
A) Detonation
B) Carburettor ice
C) A rich mixture fouling the plugs
notes.choicesExplained: B: carburettor ice restricts flow and lowers power; it does not raise cylinder head temperature. C: the mixture here is lean, not rich.
notes.explanation: High power, an excessively lean mixture and a steep climb with reduced cooling are all listed causes, and high cylinder head temperature characterises detonation.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Combustion”, p. 7-19
notes.evidence: Detonation is characterized by high cylinder head temperatures

notes.front: A cracked spark plug insulator glows hot enough to light the charge before the spark fires. What is this called?
notes.back: B) Preignition.
notes.choices:
A) Detonation
B) Preignition
C) Vapour lock
notes.choicesExplained: A: detonation is explosive burning of the charge, not ignition before the normal event. C: vapour lock stops fuel reaching the cylinders.
notes.explanation: Ignition before the normal ignition event, from a hot spot such as a cracked insulator, is preignition.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Combustion”, p. 7-19
notes.evidence: Preignition occurs when the fuel-air mixture ignites prior

notes.front: When should the fuel strainer be drained, and what are the samples checked for?
notes.back: Before each flight; the samples are checked visually for water and contaminants.
notes.explanation: Water and sediment are heavier than aviation fuel, so they settle in the sump at the bottom of the strainer.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Fuel Strainers, Sumps, and Drains”, p. 7-27
notes.evidence: samples should be drained and checked visually for water

notes.front: Why is water in the fuel sump hazardous?
notes.back: In cold weather it can freeze and block fuel lines; in warm weather it can flow into the carburettor and stop the engine.
notes.explanation: Never take off until all water and contaminants have been removed from the engine fuel system.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Fuel Strainers, Sumps, and Drains”, p. 7-27
notes.evidence: water can freeze and block fuel lines. In warm weather, it

notes.front: Your first fuel sample from a wing sump has a clear bead of water at the bottom. What do you do?
notes.back: C) Keep draining samples until no trace of water appears before flying.
notes.choices:
A) Fly: one sample with water is normal
B) Start the engine and run it to burn off the water
C) Keep draining samples until no trace of water appears before flying
notes.choicesExplained: A: water in the sump makes more water in the tanks probable. B: water in the fuel system can stop the engine, so it is removed before takeoff, not run through.
notes.explanation: If contaminants appear in the first sample, further samples are drained until no trace appears, and no takeoff is made until all water is removed.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Fuel Contamination”, p. 7-28
notes.evidence: other contaminants are found in the first sample, drain further

notes.front: What colour is 100LL aviation gasoline?
notes.back: Blue.
notes.explanation: Dyes are added because using the correct fuel is critical; 100LL performs like grade 100 but has a low lead content.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Fuel Grades”, p. 7-27
notes.evidence: 100VLL is blue like 100LL and virtually indistinguishable.

notes.front: If the proper fuel grade is not available, what may you use?
notes.back: The next higher grade; never a grade lower than recommended.
notes.explanation: A lower grade can push cylinder head and oil temperatures beyond their normal ranges, which may result in detonation.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Fuel Grades”, p. 7-27
notes.evidence: is not available, use the next higher grade as a substitute. Never

notes.front: Your engine is approved for 100LL. The only pump at a remote field sells red grade 80. What does the handbook say?
notes.back: B) Do not use it: never use a grade lower than recommended.
notes.choices:
A) Use it for one flight, then return to 100LL
B) Do not use it: never use a grade lower than recommended
C) Use it but lean the mixture to compensate
notes.choicesExplained: A: a lower grade can overheat the engine and may cause detonation, even on one flight. C: an excessively lean mixture at high power is itself a cause of detonation.
notes.explanation: Only the proper grade or the next higher one may be used; grade 80, the red fuel, is lower than 100LL.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Fuel Grades”, p. 7-27
notes.evidence: use a grade lower than recommended. This can cause the

notes.front: Why must the exhaust system be in good condition and free of cracks?
notes.back: Exhaust gases contain large amounts of carbon monoxide, which is odourless, colourless and deadly.
notes.explanation: Its presence is virtually impossible to detect, so the system must expel the gases properly.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Exhaust Systems”, p. 7-18
notes.evidence: Exhaust gases contain large amounts of carbon monoxide

notes.front: On a winter flight with the cabin heat on, you and your passenger both develop headaches and feel drowsy. Which aircraft system should you suspect?
notes.back: A) The exhaust-shroud cabin heater leaking carbon monoxide.
notes.choices:
A) The exhaust-shroud cabin heater leaking carbon monoxide
B) The pitot heat
C) The fuel strainer
notes.choicesExplained: B: pitot heat warms the pitot tube electrically and does not feed the cabin. C: the strainer removes water and sediment from the fuel and has no link to cabin air.
notes.explanation: Cabin heat in most light aircraft is air warmed around the exhaust muffler, and exhaust gases contain large amounts of carbon monoxide.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Exhaust Systems”, p. 7-18
notes.evidence: Exhaust gases contain large amounts of carbon monoxide

notes.front: What does the aircraft battery provide?
notes.back: Power for starting the engine, and a limited supply of power if the alternator fails.
notes.explanation: The alternator normally keeps the battery charged.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Electrical System”, p. 7-30
notes.evidence: starting the engine and a limited supply of electrical power

notes.front: What does a minus indication on the ammeter mean?
notes.back: More current is being drawn from the battery than is being replaced.
notes.explanation: The battery is running down, so the electrical load is exceeding what the charging system supplies.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Electrical System”, p. 7-31
notes.evidence: A minus indication means more current is being drawn

notes.front: What does a full-scale minus deflection of the ammeter indicate?
notes.back: A malfunction of the alternator.
notes.explanation: The POH gives the action to take.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Electrical System”, p. 7-31
notes.evidence: A full-scale minus deflection indicates a malfunction of the alternator/generator.

notes.front: What does a full-scale positive deflection of the ammeter indicate?
notes.back: A malfunction of the voltage regulator.
notes.explanation: The regulator controls the rate of charge to the battery by stabilising the alternator’s output.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Electrical System”, p. 7-31
notes.evidence: A full-scale positive deflection indicates a malfunction of

notes.front: When the alternator fails in flight, what should you do first, and then plan?
notes.back: Immediately shed non-essential electrical loads, then plan to land at the nearest suitable airport.
notes.explanation: Once the alternator is off line the battery is the only source, and it may last very little time.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 18, “Electrical System”, p. 18-13
notes.evidence: It is essential, therefore, that the pilot immediately shed non-essential loads when the generating source fails. [Figure 18-9] The pilot should then plan to land at the nearest suitable airport.

notes.front: At night, 40 minutes from home, your ammeter shows a full-scale minus deflection. What should you do?
notes.back: C) Shed non-essential electrical load and land at the nearest suitable airport.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing yet: the battery will run everything until home
B) Turn on all lights so the battery charges faster
C) Shed non-essential electrical load and land at the nearest suitable airport
notes.choicesExplained: A: a full-scale minus shows the alternator has failed, and the battery may last very little time. B: a higher load drains the battery faster; it cannot charge without the alternator.
notes.explanation: A full-scale minus deflection means an alternator malfunction, and the battery then supplies everything, so load is shed and a landing planned at once.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 18, “Electrical System”, p. 18-13
notes.evidence: It is essential, therefore, that the pilot immediately shed non-essential loads when the generating source fails.

notes.front: After start, how soon should oil pressure reach at least its lower limit in most conditions, and what if it does not?
notes.back: Within 30 seconds; if it does not reach the POH values in time, shut the engine down immediately.
notes.explanation: If the oil pressure limits are not reached and maintained, serious internal engine damage is likely.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 2, “Engine Starting”, p. 2-16
notes.evidence: In most conditions, oil pressure should rise to at least the lower limit within 30 seconds. To prevent damage, the engine should be shut down immediately if the oil pressure does not rise to the AFM/POH values within the required time.

notes.front: How long should the starter be run continuously, and what then?
notes.back: No more than 30 seconds, followed by a cool-down of at least 30 seconds to 1 minute.
notes.explanation: Starter motors are not designed for continuous duty; heat from a long or difficult start can damage them, and some POHs specify longer cool-downs.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 2, “Engine Starting”, p. 2-16
notes.evidence: Avoid continuous starter operation for periods longer than 30 seconds without a cool down period of at least 30 seconds to 1 minute

notes.front: Besides the onboard battery, how can electrical power for starting be supplied?
notes.back: By external power through an external power receptacle.
notes.explanation: A ground power unit is especially useful in cold weather; the manufacturer’s recommendations for starting with one are followed.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Starting System”, p. 7-18
notes.evidence: battery, but can also be supplied by external power through

notes.front: You start the engine on a cold morning. Forty seconds later the oil pressure gauge still shows nothing. What do you do?
notes.back: B) Shut the engine down immediately.
notes.choices:
A) Add power so the pump turns faster
B) Shut the engine down immediately
C) Taxi out: it will rise once the oil warms
notes.choicesExplained: A: high rpm with insufficient lubrication adds wear. C: if the limits are not reached and maintained, serious internal damage is likely.
notes.explanation: Oil pressure should reach at least its lower limit within about 30 seconds; if not, the engine is shut down to prevent damage.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 2, “Engine Starting”, p. 2-16
notes.evidence: To prevent damage, the engine should be shut down immediately if the oil pressure does not rise to the AFM/POH values within the required time.

notes.front: What is the before-takeoff check?
notes.back: The systematic POH procedure for checking the engine, controls, systems, instruments and avionics before flight.
notes.explanation: It is normally done after taxiing to a run-up position near the takeoff end of the runway.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 2, “Before-Takeoff Check”, p. 2-21
notes.evidence: The before-takeoff check is the systematic AFM/POH procedure for checking the engine, controls, systems, instruments, and avionics prior to flight.

notes.front: Above what altitude must an installed oxygen system use masks instead of cannulas?
notes.back: 18,000 feet: oxygen systems installed and certified for use above it must have masks, not cannulas.
notes.explanation: Cannulas are more comfortable but may not provide an adequate flow as reliably as masks at higher altitudes.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Cannula”, p. 7-38
notes.evidence: above 18,000 feet to be equipped with oxygen masks instead

notes.front: Are anti-icing and deicing systems meant to let you stay in icing conditions?
notes.back: No. They are not intended to sustain long-term flight in icing; structural ice needs immediate action.
notes.explanation: Their operation should be checked before any icing is encountered.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Other Anti-Ice and Deice Systems”, p. 7-41
notes.evidence: deicing equipment are not intended to sustain long-term flight

notes.front: Which is anti-ice and which is deice: carburettor heat, or inflatable wing boots that crack off built-up ice?
notes.back: Carburettor heat is anti-ice; inflatable boots are deice.
notes.explanation: Carburettor heat is described as an anti-icing system; boots remove ice after it builds on the leading edge.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Airfoil Anti-Ice and Deice”, p. 7-40
notes.evidence: leading edge, an engine-driven pneumatic pump inflates the rubber boots.

notes.front: For an aeroplane fitted with a ballistic parachute, what must an applicant know under the airman certification standards?
notes.back: When to deploy it and the associated passenger briefings.
notes.explanation: The standards also list the risks of using a ballistic parachute system and simulated deployment as a skill.
notes.source: Private Pilot for Airplane Category Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-6C), “IX. Emergency Operations, Task D. Emergency Equipment and Survival Gear”, PDF p. 62
notes.evidence: When to deploy a ballistic parachute and associated passenger briefings, if equipped.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: For an aeroplane with an emergency auto-land system, what must an applicant know under the airman certification standards?
notes.back: When to activate it and how to brief passengers on it.
notes.explanation: The standards also list the risks of using an emergency auto-land system, if one is installed.
notes.source: Private Pilot for Airplane Category Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-6C), “IX. Emergency Operations, Task D. Emergency Equipment and Survival Gear”, PDF p. 62
notes.evidence: When to activate an emergency auto-land system and brief passengers, if equipped.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How does detonation differ from preignition?
notes.back: Detonation is explosive burning of the charge; preignition is the charge lighting before the normal ignition event, usually from a hot spot.
notes.explanation: They often occur together and one may cause the other, so it is often difficult to tell them apart.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Combustion”, p. 7-20
notes.evidence: Detonation and preignition often occur simultaneously and

notes.front: How does a climb propeller differ from a cruise propeller?
notes.back: Climb: lower pitch, higher rpm, better takeoff and climb. Cruise: higher pitch, lower rpm, better cruise efficiency.
notes.explanation: Both are fixed-pitch types; which one is fitted depends on the aeroplane’s intended use.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Fixed-Pitch Propeller”, p. 7-5
notes.evidence: The climb propeller has a lower pitch, therefore less drag. Less drag results in higher rpm and more horsepower capability

notes.front: How does a gravity-feed fuel system differ from a fuel-pump system?
notes.back: Gravity feed: tanks sit above the carburettor, as in high-wing aeroplanes. Fuel pump: tanks are lower, as in low-wing aeroplanes, so pumps move the fuel.
notes.explanation: Fuel-pump systems have an engine-driven main pump and an electric auxiliary pump.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Fuel Systems”, p. 7-25
notes.evidence: to transfer fuel, fuel pumps are installed.

notes.front: How does the first sign of carburettor ice differ between a fixed-pitch and a constant-speed propeller?
notes.back: Fixed-pitch: rpm decreases. Constant-speed: manifold pressure decreases while rpm stays the same.
notes.explanation: The governor adjusts pitch to hold rpm, so the loss of power shows only on the manifold pressure gauge.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 7, “Carburetor Icing”, p. 7-10
notes.evidence: loss of power. Thus, a constant rpm is maintained.
